title: Vector Databases and Embeddings for AI Automation
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Vector Databases and Embeddings for AI Automation ##### The search that could not find the answer A company built an internal help desk automation. An employee asks a question, the system searches the policy documents and returns matching text. It used SQL `LIKE` matching. Someone typed *"how long can I be away for a medical issue?"* The policy document said *"Employees are entitled to 12 days of sick leave per calendar year."* Zero keyword overlap — no "away," no "medical," no "how long." The search returned nothing, and the ticket went to a human. That failure is not a bug in the implementation. Keyword search matches **characters**; the employee was asking about **meaning**. Bridging that gap requires representing text in a way where "medical issue" and "sick leave" are measurably close — which is exactly what embeddings do, and why they underpin every RAG system you will build. ##### What an embedding actually is An **embedding** is a fixed-length vector of floating-point numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of content. A model trained on enormous amounts of text learns to place semantically similar inputs near each other in a high-dimensional space. Concretely: OpenAI's `text-embedding-3-small` maps any text to 1,536 numbers. `"sick leave policy"` and `"medical absence rules"` land close together; `"quarterly revenue forecast"` lands far away — despite sharing no words with either. The mechanics that matter in practice: - **Dimensionality** is fixed per model (384 for many open models, 768, 1,536, or 3,072 for larger ones). Higher dimensions capture more nuance at the cost of storage and search time. - **Distance metrics** quantify closeness. **Cosine similarity** measures the angle between vectors and ignores magnitude — the standard choice for text. Euclidean (L2) and inner product are the alternatives; use whichever your model was trained for, and **be consistent**, because mixing metrics silently degrades results. - **Embeddings are model-specific.** Vectors from two different models are not comparable. Changing your embedding model means re-embedding your entire corpus. That last point has real operational weight: your embedding model is a long-term commitment, and migrating means a full reindex. ##### Semantic versus keyword search | | Keyword (BM25 / `LIKE` / full-text) | Semantic (vector) | |---|---|---| | Matches on | Exact terms, stems | Meaning | | "sick leave" finds "medical absence"? | No | Yes | | Exact SKU / error code / name | Excellent | Unreliable | | Typos and paraphrase | Poor | Robust | | Explainability | High — you see the matched term | Low | | Cost | Very low | Embedding cost + vector storage | Neither dominates. Semantic search fails on precisely the queries keyword search handles best — someone searching for order `ORD-1042` or error code `E4471` wants a literal match, and an embedding will happily return "semantically similar" order numbers, which is useless. This is why **hybrid search** is the production default: run both, then combine. **Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)** is the standard merging technique because it needs no score normalization between two incomparable scales: ```text score(doc) = Σ 1 / (k + rank_in_that_result_list) with k ≈ 60 ``` A document ranked 2nd by vector search and 5th by keyword search scores `1/62 + 1/65`, outranking something that appears only in one list. Simple, robust, and it consistently beats either method alone. ##### Chunking You do not embed whole documents. A 40-page policy PDF as one vector produces a blurry average of everything in it, matching nothing well. You split it into **chunks**, and chunking strategy affects retrieval quality more than model choice does. Guidelines that hold up in practice: - **Size: 300–800 tokens.** Too small loses context ("12 days" without knowing of what); too large dilutes the embedding and wastes context window on irrelevant text. - **Overlap: 10–20%.** Prevents a sentence spanning a boundary from being lost to both chunks. - **Split on semantic boundaries** — headings, paragraphs, sections — before falling back to character counts. A chunk that ends mid-sentence embeds poorly. - **Prepend context.** Adding the document title and section heading to each chunk's text before embedding measurably improves retrieval, because the chunk carries its own provenance. - **Store rich metadata**: source document, section, page, date, department, access level. Metadata is what makes filtering possible, and filtering is what makes retrieval precise. ##### Indexes: HNSW and IVF Comparing a query against every stored vector is **exact** but linear — fine for 10,000 vectors, hopeless for 10 million. Vector indexes trade a little accuracy for enormous speed, doing **approximate nearest neighbour (ANN)** search. **HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World)** builds a multi-layer graph where each node links to nearby neighbours. Search starts at a sparse top layer, greedily descends toward the query, and refines at the bottom. Malkov and Yashunin's 2018 paper established it as the state of the art, and it is the default in most vector databases: excellent recall, logarithmic-ish query time, higher memory use, slower build. Its two tuning parameters: `m` (connections per node — higher means better recall, more memory) and `ef_construction` (build-time search breadth). At query time, `ef_search` trades latency for recall directly. **IVFFlat** partitions vectors into clusters, then searches only the nearest few. Faster to build and lighter on memory, with lower recall. Its parameters are `lists` (number of clusters, roughly `rows/1000`) and `probes` (clusters searched per query). Practical guidance: **HNSW unless build time or memory is the binding constraint.** And note both are approximate — you can miss results. Raise `ef_search`/`probes` if recall matters more than latency. ##### pgvector in practice ```sql CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector; CREATE TABLE doc_chunks ( id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, document_id TEXT NOT NULL, section TEXT, chunk_index INT NOT NULL, content TEXT NOT NULL, embedding vector(1536) NOT NULL, department TEXT, updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), content_tsv tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector('english', content)) STORED, UNIQUE (document_id, chunk_index) ); -- HNSW index for cosine distance CREATE INDEX idx_chunks_embedding ON doc_chunks USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops) WITH (m = 16, ef_construction = 64); -- Supporting indexes for filtering and keyword search CREATE INDEX idx_chunks_department ON doc_chunks (department); CREATE INDEX idx_chunks_tsv ON doc_chunks USING GIN (content_tsv); ``` Note `vector_cosine_ops` — the operator class must match the distance operator you query with (`<=>` cosine, `<->` L2, `<#>` inner product), or Postgres silently ignores the index and does a sequential scan. Hybrid search with RRF, entirely in SQL: ```sql WITH semantic AS ( SELECT id, content, section, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY embedding <=> $1) AS rank FROM doc_chunks WHERE department = $2 -- metadata filter ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 30 ), keyword AS ( SELECT id, content, section, ROW_NUMBER() OVER ( ORDER BY ts_rank_cd(content_tsv, plainto_tsquery('english', $3)) DESC ) AS rank FROM doc_chunks WHERE department = $2 AND content_tsv @@ plainto_tsquery('english', $3) LIMIT 30 ) SELECT COALESCE(s.id, k.id) AS id, COALESCE(s.content, k.content) AS content, COALESCE(1.0 / (60 + s.rank), 0) + COALESCE(1.0 / (60 + k.rank), 0) AS rrf_score FROM semantic s FULL OUTER JOIN keyword k USING (id) ORDER BY rrf_score DESC LIMIT 8; ``` And the ingestion side: ```python import httpx, os from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI(api_key=os.environ["OPENAI_API_KEY"]) def embed_batch(texts: list[str], model: str = "text-embedding-3-small") -> list[list[float]]: """Batch embedding calls — far cheaper and faster than one-at-a-time.""" resp = client.embeddings.create(model=model, input=texts) return [d.embedding for d in resp.data] def ingest(chunks: list[dict], conn) -> None: for i in range(0, len(chunks), 100): # batch of 100 batch = chunks[i:i + 100] # Prepend context so each chunk carries its own provenance texts = [f"{c['document_title']} — {c['section']}\n\n{c['content']}" for c in batch] vectors = embed_batch(texts) with conn.cursor() as cur: cur.executemany( """ INSERT INTO doc_chunks (document_id, section, chunk_index, content, embedding, department) VALUES (%s, %s, %s, %s, %s, %s) ON CONFLICT (document_id, chunk_index) DO UPDATE SET content = EXCLUDED.content, embedding = EXCLUDED.embedding, updated_at = now() """, [(c["document_id"], c["section"], c["chunk_index"], c["content"], v, c["department"]) for c, v in zip(batch, vectors)], ) conn.commit() ``` The `ON CONFLICT` upsert makes re-ingestion idempotent — the same discipline as everywhere else, applied to embeddings. ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Documents] --> B[Chunk
300-800 tokens, 15% overlap] B --> C[Prepend title + section] C --> D[Embed in batches] D --> E[(Vector store
+ metadata + tsvector)] Q[User query] --> F[Embed query] F --> G[ANN search
+ metadata filter] Q --> H[Keyword search
BM25 / tsquery] G --> I[RRF fusion] H --> I I --> J[Optional rerank
cross-encoder] J --> K[Top-k chunks → LLM] ``` ##### pgvector versus managed vector databases **pgvector** — an extension turning Postgres into a vector store. Its decisive advantage is that **vectors live beside your relational data**, so you can join, filter with SQL `WHERE` clauses, and wrap everything in one transaction. One database to operate, back up and secure. It comfortably handles low millions of vectors. **Managed vector databases** (Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus) are purpose-built: better performance at very large scale, distributed sharding, built-in hybrid search and reranking, namespaces, and horizontal scaling without you operating it. The choice: - **pgvector** when you already run Postgres, your corpus is under a few million chunks, and you need to filter or join against relational data. This describes most automation and internal-tooling projects. - **Managed** when you have tens of millions of vectors, need very low latency at high QPS, want multi-tenant namespaces out of the box, or lack the appetite to tune index parameters. One nuance worth knowing: **filtered vector search is genuinely hard**. A restrictive `WHERE department = 'legal'` combined with an ANN index can degrade recall, because the index navigates by vector proximity and then discards non-matching rows. Purpose-built databases implement filter-aware search; with pgvector, partial indexes per high-cardinality filter or a pre-filtered subquery help. ##### Common pitfalls - **Mismatched operator class and distance operator**, silently disabling the index. - **Mixing embedding models** in one collection — the vectors are incomparable. - **Embedding whole documents** instead of chunks. - **No overlap**, losing content at chunk boundaries. - **Discarding metadata**, making filtering and citation impossible. - **One embedding call per chunk** instead of batching — slow and costly. - **Semantic-only search** for exact identifiers. - **Never evaluating retrieval.** Build a set of question/expected-chunk pairs and measure recall@k; without it you are guessing. - **Forgetting to re-embed** when documents change. - **Ignoring that ANN is approximate** and expecting exhaustive recall. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: using **pgvector or a free Qdrant/Weaviate instance**, embed a set of documents, store vectors with metadata, then embed a query and retrieve the most similar chunks — **verifying meaning-based rather than keyword matching**. Prove it deliberately: write a query that shares no words with the target passage, exactly like the sick-leave example, and confirm it still retrieves correctly. That single test is what makes the concept real. The mini project is a **semantic search service**: ingest a document set with sensible chunking, store embeddings with metadata, and expose a **FastAPI endpoint returning top-k chunks** with **metadata filtering** and **optional hybrid search**. Build a small evaluation set of twenty questions with known correct chunks and measure recall@5 before and after adding hybrid search — that measurement turns tuning from guesswork into engineering. For the assignment, explain **what an embedding is** and how **semantic search differs from keyword search**, then compare **pgvector with a managed vector database** with a scenario for each. The strongest argument for pgvector is transactional consistency and SQL filtering alongside relational data; the strongest for managed is scale plus filter-aware ANN and reranking you would otherwise build yourself. ##### Key takeaways - Embeddings map content to fixed-length vectors where proximity means semantic similarity — model-specific, so switching models requires a full reindex. - Semantic search finds meaning, keyword search finds exact terms; hybrid search fused with RRF beats either, especially for identifiers and codes. - Chunk at 300–800 tokens with 10–20% overlap on semantic boundaries, prepend title and section context, and store rich metadata for filtering and citation. - HNSW is the default ANN index (tune `m`, `ef_construction`, `ef_search`); IVFFlat is lighter and faster to build with lower recall — and both are approximate. - Choose pgvector for transactional consistency and SQL filtering under a few million vectors; choose a managed vector database for very large scale, filter-aware search and built-in reranking.
